title: How the Makers of Buddy Turned a Unicorn Into a Surprise Hit
summary: Sometimes, a movie appears seemingly out of nowhere and instantly captures everyone's imagination. In 2026, one of those movies was Buddy, a horror comedy by Casper Kelly about a 1990s TV show mascot with a dark side. What made Buddy stand out, according to the people who made it, was not just the jokes or the scares. It was the emotional depth underneath. Buddy the Unicorn has humour and charm, but also a darker side and remorse for his actions. That mix allowed the film's team to build a very unusual marketing campaign. Roadside Attractions introduced audiences to the character first, before letting them know about his darker side. The campaign created a false memory that led many people to wonder if Buddy was actually a cancelled TV show they had forgotten about. By the time audiences learned what the film was really about, they were already invested in the character. At IndieWire's Future of Filmmaking Summit in Los Angeles, Buddy producer Tracy Rosenblum, co-writer Jamie King, and Roadside Attractions head of digital marketing Melissa Yerou talked about the years of behind-the-scenes work that goes into an overnight success. The project began as a way to put Kelly's distinct brand of comedy into a feature film. King was brought in as co-writer to help fit Kelly's wild ideas into a movie format, using his experience writing Disney movies to add enough heart to reach a wider audience. King said he knew Kelly would make it really funny, and his friends at BoulderLight would make it really scary, so if he could help bring the heart element, that would check all three boxes for a great movie. He and Kelly worked hard to make Buddy a three-dimensional character who contained both light and darkness. Kelly was clear that Buddy was not just a fuzzy villain, but someone who could be a good person yet had gone down the wrong road. Rosenblum, laughing, said Buddy has depth and shame, and is not a good guy, but that is what makes him special. The character was so well developed that Yerou's marketing team could hit the ground running. They had Buddy interact with classic 1990s brands on social media, and audiences fell in love with the voice King and Kelly had worked so hard to refine. At first, the team responded to every comment, and soon people were commenting just because they wanted Buddy to respond.
why_it_matters: It shows how a film can win an audience by building a character people care about first, and how jokes, scares, and heart can work together in one story.
